text.text: Shared code, including the data generators and the plot theme, is in R/helpers.R. The seven studies comprise 18 180 design cells and took about 67 hours to run on ten M4 cores.
Each study uses a resumable runner.

Design cells are keyed on the columns of the design grid, results are checkpointed to disk after every chunk, and cells already present in the cache are skipped, so raising a replication count and rerunning computes only the new cells.
Seeds are deterministic functions of the design cell rather than of the execution order, which means any single cell can be reproduced on its own without running the study that contains it.
All results were produced with R 4.6.1 (R Core Team, 2026) and easyRasch2 (Johansson, 2026a), under versions 1.1.0 and 1.1.1 and, for the two dichotomous studies, 1.4.0.

Taking 99% of that reference width as a criterion, 1000 iterations suffice for 𝑤 = .95, 2000 for 𝑤 = .99, and 5000 for 𝑤 = .999.

Note the different y-axis scales for the two rows.Figure3compares all four rules at the anchored misfit level.

Against the interval at 𝑤 = .999 the WY rule detects substantially more misfit, by 8.8 to 18.3 percentage points across the non-saturated nine-item conditions at 𝐵 = 2000, at a false positive rate of 1.2% against 0.6% for the interval, pooled across arms, so it detects more at a higher cost.
Part of this raw gain, however, reflects the interval's implicit error rate rather than the method.

By Equation 1, 𝑤 = .999 corresponds to a familywise rate of only 0.9% for nine items, so the interval is operating far below the 𝛼 = .05 of the p-value rules.A fair comparison holds the error rate constant.
For nine items, 𝑤 = .995 implies a familywise rate of 4.4% by Equation 1, and its observed null rate at 𝐵 = 2000 was 5.3%, closely matching the p-value rules.
Against this matched interval the WY rule still detected more misfit in every non-saturated condition, by 1.7 to 5.0 percentage points, with slightly fewer false positives.
The remaining advantage comes from studentization and from using the joint distribution of the item statistics.

More important than its size is what the matching exercise reveals: an interval width that matches a chosen 𝛼 must be solved from Equation1for each item count, and for most item counts no convenient width exists.
The WY rule targets 𝛼 directly, whatever the number of items.TableS4reports Holm by condition.
At 𝐵 = 100 it detected 0.0% of the misfitting items, since the floor of Equation 4 is 180 iterations for nine items and 300 for fifteen.

At 𝐵 = 2000 the WY rule detected between -1.7 and 1.7 percentage points more than Holm across conditions, paired within replications, with standard errors of up to 2.0 points, and the pooled false positive rates were 1.2% against 1.0%.
Using the joint distribution of the item statistics therefore adds little power here, asFerreira's (2024) account leads one to expect for statistics that are close to independent.

text.text: The practical advantage of the step-down over Holm is that it needs no minimum number of iterations.A short scale tests BH where the floor does not bind at all.
At five items the floor is 100 iterations, so the procedure operates freely at every 𝐵 examined, and the comparison is no longer handicapped by reachability.
At 𝑛 = 250 it detected the misfitting item in 91.2% of replications
Figure 4.
Seed dependence of flagging decisions Note.

Percentage of items whose flagging decision depends on the bootstrap seed (25 seeds per dataset, 10 datasets per condition), by number of iterations, misfit severity, decision rule, item set, and sample size.
Lower values of the inter-dimensional correlation mean stronger misfit.
Percondition values carry Monte Carlo standard errors of up to about 3 percentage points and are tabulated in TableS8.
Figure4shows that instability is not monotone in misfit severity or sample size.
At 𝐵 = 2000 the strongest misfit (𝜌 = .15) left on average 1.1 items per dataset with a seed-dependent flag at 𝑛 = 250 but 0.0 at 𝑛 = 1000, where items were flagged or cleared decisively.

Instability arises where the evidence about an item approaches the flagging threshold without clearly passing it, so it is driven by the number of such boundary items rather than by misfit severity or sample size as such.
Across the misfit conditions, the probability that two seeds disagreed at 𝐵 = 2000 ranged from 0 to 23%.
With ten datasets per condition, these results illustrate the dependence rather than giving rates that carry over to other data.How much instability an analysis shows is thus set by the data.
